sentences.text: Who decides what runs next in a self-driving lab?
Self-driving laboratories, or SDLs, automate experiments and use the results to choose what to test next.
Language-model agents such as Coscientist and ACRA have already run robotic experiments.
Worldwide — from Canada's Acceleration Consortium to the US Genesis Mission and Japan's ARiSE programme — efforts are under way to build and scale SDL infrastructure.
Cloud laboratories already let researchers share instruments remotely, without owning a lab.
As this grows, a single facility could run many experiments at once — hundreds of instruments, nearly a hundred robot arms, and a fleet of mobile robots moving samples between them.
But scale doesn't make resources unlimited.
Instruments, robot arms, floor space and time are all finite, and experiments compete for the same equipment and transport.
Every lab needs a scheduler and resource manager — deciding what to install, and what to run first.
How do we know whether that decision-maker is any good?
We built LabOpsBench: a benchmark that runs an agent's decisions inside a simulated laboratory, with instruments, robot arms, mobile robots, queues and finite buffers.
It simulates operations — not chemistry.
At time zero, the agent sees every unfinished job — including future arrivals, with dependencies and durations — plus the room layout and resource limits.
It picks an equipment configuration from shared candidates and gives each job a priority.
The engine validates the decision, dispatches operations and moves the robots.
Every 1,800 simulated seconds, the agent can re-prioritise or request a permitted equipment exchange.
The score is makespan — time until the last sample is unloaded.
Unfinished runs get no score.
To ground the workloads, we turned public LeMat-Synth annotations — synthesis procedures extracted from the literature — into eight scheduling templates.
They power fourteen scenarios, from small cells to a hall with 32 instruments, 32 arms and 64 jobs.
Here are two agents on the same task: twelve jobs — six five-step chains and six single mixing jobs.
GPT-6 Luna's plan: feed the oven pipeline first.
It ranks the long chains on top, keeps the layout, and pushes those chains through.
Jev gets exactly the same observation and candidates.
Instead of a fixed order, it keeps revising its ranking across seventeen decisions, mixing the two job types as the lab changes.
Same lab, same jobs — different strategies.
We also built a web interface for every recorded run.
On this task, Luna finished in 8.27 hours, Jev in 8.33, and first-in-first-out took 12.6.
The best method changes by task: on compact lab layouts, Jev and a workload-aware algorithm beat Luna.
Click any result to replay it in 2D or 3D and step through each decision.
Playback only reads recorded engine events — it never changes the score.
Today, LabOpsBench scores time.
But future labs will need to weigh much more — scarce elements, electricity, water — in one combined decision.
LabOpsBench is a foundation for evaluating those trade-offs, and for testing our simulation against real laboratories.
